questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The first question about a document
questions.learningObjective: identify the purpose-first question to ask of a source
questions.stem: A government clerk compiled this register partly to show that a new levy on grain was justified. Which question should a historian ask before reading its figures?

options.text: How many other registers from the same office survive
options.misconception: believes a count of copies settles what a record means

options.text: Who wrote it, for whom, and what outcome it was meant to produce
How consistently the totals are written from page to page
options.misconception: believes internal neatness is the first test of a record

options.text: How widely the clerk's opinion was shared by contemporaries
options.misconception: measures an author's reach instead of the author's purpose

questions.explanation: Every document is a person's answer to a question, and a register written to justify a levy will be shaped to make the need look pressing and the yield look adequate, so the author, the audience, and the purpose have to be fixed before the numbers mean anything. The tempting options ask about the archive's size, the writing's tidiness, and the clerk's reach, and none of those touches the stake the writer had in the outcome.
questions.hint: What did the writer want the reader to conclude?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: evaluate whether two agreeing accounts are independent
questions.stem: Two official reports on the same uprising use nearly identical wording, and each credits a newspaper that appeared first. How should their agreement be weighed?

options.text: As one piece of evidence, because both repeat a single earlier account
As two independent checks that confirm the reported sequence
options.misconception: believes matching wording proves the accounts were independent

options.text: As proof that the newspaper account was free of error
options.misconception: treats one early account as the standard all copies must match

options.text: As evidence that the two offices secretly coordinated their reporting
options.misconception: reads shared phrasing as proof of a conspiracy

questions.explanation: Corroboration raises confidence only when the accounts could have failed independently, and two reports that copy one newspaper share a single set of errors, so this agreement measures circulation rather than confirmation. The tempting options read matching phrases as independent checking, treat the first account as the standard all copies must meet, and see conspiracy in wording that may simply descend from one source.
questions.hint: Where did the shared wording come from?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a customs register can establish
questions.learningObjective: limit a document's claim to the job it was created for
questions.stem: A surviving register from a medieval customs house lists bolts of dyed cloth with the duty set against each, and records nothing else. What can that register establish?

options.text: What the officials recorded as dutiable, not what was traded
The total volume of cloth that passed through the town
options.misconception: reads a list of assessed goods as a complete trade count

options.text: Which merchants hid bolts from the customs officers
options.misconception: infers deliberate evasion from a document silent on it

options.text: The ordinary working dress of the town's inhabitants
options.misconception: reads a customs entry as evidence about everyday clothing

questions.explanation: A customs register is made to fix a liability, so it records the goods an officer assessed and a duty was set against them, and the trades that avoided assessment leave no row behind at all. The tempting options read the list as a census of the trade, as an accusation against named smugglers, and as evidence about how people dressed, when the document answers only the question the collectors were paid to answer.
questions.hint: What job was this register created to do?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: use a text's genre to bound what it can show
questions.stem: A ruler's proclamation announcing a pardon after a revolt praises the ruler's mercy and reports the rebels as penitent. What does the genre of that text establish most securely?

options.text: That the ruler's merciful self-image was being proclaimed
That the pardon was never actually carried out in the districts
options.misconception: reads a public proclamation as proof of non-implementation

options.text: That the rebels had committed crimes the text passes over
options.misconception: infers omitted atrocities from a document written to end them

options.text: That clemency after a revolt was a fixed legal requirement
options.misconception: assumes a legal rule the text neither states nor implies

questions.explanation: A proclamation is an instrument of public persuasion, so the most secure inference concerns the image its author was building, since a ruler announcing mercy after a revolt is claiming a virtue before an audience. The tempting options treat the text as an operational record of implementation, as a confession of hidden crimes, and as evidence of a standing legal rule, when the genre licenses only the claim about the proclaimed self-image.
questions.hint: Who was the audience for this text?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Judging the past by its own moment
questions.learningObjective: recognize anachronism in a historical judgment
questions.stem: A scholar faults a thirteenth-century ruler for founding no hospital, even though the institution did not yet exist. What is the flaw in that judgment?

options.text: It applies a standard the ruler's own century could not set
It mistakes a hospital for the only form of medical charity
options.misconception: believes modern institutions were the sole form of earlier care

options.text: It assumes the ruler was judged by courts of his own day
options.misconception: supposes ancient judges enforced present-day expectations

options.text: It treats a missing building as a deliberate refusal by the ruler
options.misconception: reads an absence of record as proof of a chosen omission

questions.explanation: Judgment requires a standard the moment could recognize, and where an institution does not yet exist its absence cannot show neglect, so the critic measures the past against a possibility that had not arrived. The tempting options claim that medical charity took only the later form, that ancient judges applied modern expectations, and that no building means the ruler chose against one, none of which follows from the date of the institution.
questions.hint: Could the ruler have founded one?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: read what a spending series says once totals are compared with headcounts
questions.stem: A garrison account book lists 1,200 men costing 12,000 a year in 1540, then 1,220 men costing 36,000 a year in 1560. What does that pair of entries show?

options.text: The extra money bought upkeep and equipment, not more men
The garrison expanded steadily across the two decades
options.misconception: reads a 1.7 percent headcount rise as substantial expansion

options.text: The books simply record a war's costs after the fighting
options.misconception: treats a rising bill as a delayed payment for a past war

options.text: Every rise in the bill is explained by rising prices alone
options.misconception: assumes one invisible cause so the figures cannot test it

questions.explanation: Cost per man moves from 10 to about 29.5 a year while the headcount barely shifts, so a tripled bill has to be pay, food, and equipment rather than soldiers, since a rise in headcount would have shown in the roster. The tempting options read the flat roster as expansion, treat a rising total as a settled war bill, and hide the change behind prices, which would predict a different pattern in the roster than the one recorded.
questions.hint: Divide each year's bill by the men it covers.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: identify a map's uniform fill as a claim rather than a measurement
questions.stem: A court map paints a scattered set of provinces in one flat color and prints no legend of conquest. What kind of claim is that coloring making?

options.text: An argument that the realm is one and must be held together
A record of which provinces had been conquered by force
options.misconception: reads a color choice as a report of military action

options.text: A measure of how wealthy each province happened to be
options.misconception: infers an economic ranking from a uniform fill

options.text: A notice that the cartographer had never visited the region
options.misconception: treats a missing legend as evidence of the mapmaker's travels

questions.explanation: A single flat color suppresses the border lines and the dates that would show separate conquests, so the map presents political wholeness to an audience that must be persuaded of it, which makes the coloring a claim rather than a measurement. The tempting options read the fill as a record of force, as a ranking of wealth, and as an admission of ignorance, none of which is information a color can carry.
questions.hint: What does the map choose not to show?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: read a place-name as a record of a claim rather than of settlement
questions.stem: After a conquest, settlers renamed a bay after a minister at home while local speakers kept the older name for the same water. What does the newer name record?

options.text: Which power claimed the place, not who lived there first
That the earlier inhabitants had no settled life of their own
options.misconception: reads a colonial name as evidence that nobody was there

options.text: That the two names refer to different bodies of water
options.misconception: treats one place as two because its names differ

options.text: That the older name was legally abolished by the new authority
options.misconception: assumes a renaming ended the local name in use

questions.explanation: A renamed place carries the new authority's claim onto the map, since the naming power expects its own names to be the ones written down, while continued local use shows that the claim was contested rather than complete. The tempting options read the new name as proof nobody was there before, as evidence of two different waters, and as a legal abolition of the old name, none of which a change of name by itself establishes.
questions.hint: Whose name is being written down, and whose is not?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: identify what a rendering of a diplomatic formula can lose
questions.stem: A treaty translated into a modern language promises to share land between two kinsmen as brothers share a field. Reasoning from the translation alone risks which error?

options.text: Reading a formula of goodwill as a description of division
Missing a legal term whose sense was already fixed and exact
options.misconception: believes treaty vocabulary held one settled legal meaning

options.text: Trusting a rendering that carries no choices of its own
options.misconception: assumes any translation reproduces the words exactly

options.text: Discarding a clause because its words seem imprecise
options.misconception: treats an imprecise rendering as grounds to ignore the promise

questions.explanation: Diplomatic formulas are chosen for what they leave unstated, so a promise to share as brothers sets a manner of holding without a measurable division, and a modern rendering cannot supply the terms that were left out. The tempting options assume a fixed legal sense, treat translation as choice-free, and dismiss the clause as too vague, when the vagueness here is exactly what the negotiators meant to achieve.
questions.hint: What work is the formula doing for the negotiators?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: weigh a memoir composed long after the events it describes
questions.stem: An officer's memoir of a campaign was written thirty years after it, when the war's outcome and his own disgrace were both settled. How should the memoir be read?

options.text: As memory and justification mixed by a writer with a stake
As worthless, because a memory written so late cannot be trusted
options.misconception: believes the age of a memoir alone voids every detail

options.text: As neutral, because the writer had been present at the events
options.misconception: equates eyewitness presence with an unpartial record

options.text: As a record of what the officer believed at the time itself
options.misconception: reads a later justification as a transparent record of earlier belief

questions.explanation: Writing thirty years on means the author now knows how it ended and has reason to defend a reputation, so recollection and self-justification arrive already shaped by that knowledge. The tempting options throw the whole account away because of the delay, grant neutrality on the strength of presence alone, and read the later defense as though it were the earlier belief unchanged.
questions.hint: What did the writer know that his soldiers did not?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain how preservation habits shape what a record contains
questions.stem: Almost everything preserved from a medieval abbey is letters, grants, and accounts, and none of it is the talk of the field workers. What follows for a historian?

options.text: The record will overstate the concerns of those who wrote
That field workers led lives far simpler than the abbey suggests
options.misconception: infers simplicity from the absence of their recorded words

options.text: That documents mentioning them were deliberately destroyed
options.misconception: treats a gap in the archive as an act of destruction

options.text: That the abbey once kept records of every kind of voice
options.misconception: assumes a lost file once held what the archive lacks

questions.explanation: What survives is what someone thought worth copying, and the abbey's paper reflects the concerns of clerics, landlords, and officials, so a history built only from it will treat those concerns as the whole of the period. The tempting options turn the silence into evidence about the workers' lives, into a destruction story, and into a promise of a fuller archive, none of which the record can carry.
questions.hint: Who had a reason to write things down?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Designing a test of a dating
questions.learningObjective: design a check on an archaeological date drawn from disturbed material
questions.stem: A curator dates a masonry ruin to about 700 from one coin found in a layer a looter admits he disturbed. Which step would best test the date?

options.text: Seek undisturbed layers with datable material above and below
Ask the looter where else he saw coins that morning
options.misconception: takes a self-reported spot as an undisturbed context

options.text: Date every object in the collection from that same coin
options.misconception: makes one uncertain object the reference for everything

options.text: Assume the coin dates the ruin since coins stay where found
options.misconception: believes objects cannot move within a single layer

questions.explanation: A disturbed layer destroys the one thing a coin can give, its secure relationship to the walls, so the test has to restore that relationship by finding datable material sealed between undisturbed deposits. The tempting options shift the problem to a collector's memory, spread a single uncertain date across the whole collection, and assume objects cannot move, each of which keeps the shaky date instead of checking it.
questions.hint: What did the looter's admission remove?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: sequence the moves of a source critique in a workable order
questions.stem: Four moves in working on a suspect record are described. Which sequence best fits the order a careful critic uses?

options.text: Check the claims against independent records outside the text
options.misconception: jumps outside before the text's own identity and date are known

options.text: Establish when it was written and for what audience
options.misconception: tests for bias before knowing when or for whom it was written

options.text: Weigh the claims within the text for bias and contradiction
options.misconception: accepts internal agreement without any outside comparison

options.text: Look for separate accounts that confirm the same details
options.misconception: counts matching details without asking where the second came from

questions.explanation: Criticism has an order because each step answers to the one before it: identity and date fix which version of the text is in hand, internal weighing sets its reliability, outside comparison tests it, and only then does agreement with separate accounts add weight. The tempting orders judge bias before dating the text, skip the outside comparison altogether, or accept matching details without asking whether the second account is independent.
questions.hint: Which step needs the answer from the step before it?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: read a clustering of round figures as an answering pattern
questions.stem: Of 400 household returns on a government income form, 260 report income as a round multiple of fifty and the remaining 140 give an ending figure. What does the pattern show?

options.text: Respondents reported figures that matched the form's bands
That the clerks invented most of the figures themselves
options.misconception: explains clustered answers by inventing a forger's habit

options.text: That household incomes really came in round multiples only
options.misconception: reads an answering pattern as a fact about earnings

options.text: That the form sampled households at random from every rank
options.misconception: believes random sampling would produce clustered answers

questions.explanation: Round endings in 65 percent of the returns, where genuine earnings scatter, show respondents fitting their answers to the bands the form offered, so the figures record the shape of the questionnaire as much as the households. The tempting options invent a clerk's forgery, treat the clustering as a fact about incomes, and expect a random sample to produce the pattern, which is the opposite of what random sampling looks like.
questions.hint: What would scattered real earnings look like?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A record and a memory compared
questions.learningObjective: combine an institutional record and an oral memory without forcing agreement
questions.stem: A temple's stone ledger lists grain deliveries for three years, and villagers' songs recall a shortage in the third. Which reading uses both sources best?

options.text: The ledger shows what the temple received, the songs how it was lived
Both must describe the same year, so one of them is wrong
options.misconception: assumes two records of an event cannot differ in kind

options.text: The songs are credible only where the stone is missing
options.misconception: makes oral memory usable only as a gap-filler

options.text: The ledger settles what ordinary households actually ate
options.misconception: treats a temple's intake as a household diet survey

questions.explanation: A stone ledger and a recited memory are different instruments aimed at different questions, one at what passed the temple gate and one at how a shortage was borne, so their detail and their silence do not compete. The tempting options require the two to match, restrict the songs to filling gaps, and read an institutional intake as a household diet, which loses exactly what each source holds.
questions.hint: What was each record made to do?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: draw a licensed conclusion from a documentary silence
questions.stem: A town's surviving archive contains no mention of a famine that later chronicles describe in detail. Which conclusion is defensible?

options.text: The archive's silence is a fact about the archive itself
That no famine occurred, since the town kept careful records
options.misconception: takes an administrative habit as a guarantee of coverage

options.text: That the chronicles invented the famine to embarrass the town
options.misconception: assumes a motive for invention without any internal clue

options.text: That the archive was destroyed specifically to hide the famine
options.misconception: converts a missing file into deliberate concealment

questions.explanation: A gap in an archive reports what its keepers wrote down, not what happened, and a shortage severe enough to be remembered later may simply have fallen outside what a town office wrote. The tempting options read the gap as absence of the event, invent a motive for the later chronicles, and treat the missing file as proof of deliberate destruction, none of which the silence can carry.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: judge how far an internal contradiction damages a document
questions.stem: A report calls a general fearless, then says he refused every cavalry charge because he doubted the ground. Which criticism fits the case best?

options.text: The contradiction weakens the whole report, not just one line
Only the cavalry passages are doubtful, the praise still stands
options.misconception: saves a document by excising the parts that fail it

options.text: The report must be forged, since a real writer would not praise
options.misconception: treats mixed judgment as proof of deliberate falsification

options.text: Mixed praise and caution is normal in reports and proves nothing
options.misconception: declares a document uncriticizable because such mixtures are common

questions.explanation: A text that praises a quality and then describes conduct denying it is pulling in two directions, and until that strain is explained the reporter's reliability is in question across the document rather than in one passage. The tempting options exempt the praise, declare the text forged because genuine praise and caution do not mix, and dismiss the contradiction because such mixtures are ordinary in reports.
questions.hint: Does one flaw stay inside one line?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: use the distance between two accounts as evidence about a measure
questions.stem: A king's chronicle calls a new levy blessed and a gift to the realm, while a merchant's letter says the same levy took a full year's profit. What does the pair establish?

options.text: The gap between the two accounts is the levy's real cost
The merchant's letter must be false, since the levy was lawful
options.misconception: settles a source question by the legality of the measure

options.text: The chronicle is worthless, being nothing but praise of rulers
options.misconception: dismisses a whole genre instead of weighing its claims

options.text: Only the chronicle shows what the state actually collected
options.misconception: assumes praise sits nearer a receipt than a complaint does

The tempting options resolve the disagreement by legality, dismiss the chronicle wholesale as flattery, and prefer the celebratory account as though praise were closer to a receipt than a complaint is.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A census as an administrative act
questions.learningObjective: read a register's categories as evidence of its purpose
questions.stem: An 1750 census names every household head as an employed man, while parish registers list many widows heading their own households. What does the discrepancy show?

options.text: The census recorded who counted for tax and liability
The parish registers were filled in with deliberate falsehoods
options.misconception: assigns a motive to the registers the sources do not report

options.text: Women really did never head a household in that decade

options.text: The census was built to count people, so the registers must be wrong
options.misconception: assumes a stated purpose when the form contradicts it

questions.topic: Planning a check of a claim
questions.learningObjective: design a test that does not depend on the claimant's own documents
questions.stem: A student must test whether a ruler's reign really raised grain output. Which plan would give the strongest test?

options.text: Compare dated harvest records kept by several institutions
Trust the one chronicle that praises the reign's abundance
options.misconception: rests the whole test on the most flattering witness

options.text: Count the ruler's own inscriptions praising good harvests
options.misconception: makes the claimant's own monuments the measure

options.text: Use the grain price alone, since prices are never distorted
options.misconception: accepts a single unexamined proxy as a complete measure

questions.topic: The limits of a customs book
questions.learningObjective: compute a recorded shortfall and state what the record can support
questions.stem: A customs book shows 900 loads declared at the frontier in 1462 with 610 logged inside the city, then 1,600 declared in 1502 with 1,500 inside. What follows?

That smuggling had ended altogether by the year 1502

options.misconception: treats a border declaration as a count of goods that moved

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Oral tradition and layers of collection
questions.learningObjective: separate inherited material from a later layer of recording
questions.stem: A region's epic was recorded by a nineteenth-century collector, and the recorded text carries place-names and a closing prayer in forms no longer current. What does the record hold?

options.text: Older inherited material under a later layer of collection
The oldest recoverable wording of the story, unaltered by time
options.misconception: treats a recorded version as the earliest form of the tradition

options.text: Proof the story was invented by the collector from local place-names
options.misconception: attributes authorship to the collector on the strength of names

options.text: Only printed versions are usable, since writing fixes a text
options.misconception: ranks printed text above any living recitation as record

questions.explanation: A collected text carries two layers at once, the older material of a recited tradition and the later work of transcription, translation, and editing by the collector, and the current forms of names and prayer mark the later edge. The tempting options make the collected text the original, blame the collector for inventing the story because of his place-names, and dismiss any text not fixed in print, each confusing the recording with the tradition itself.
questions.hint: Which part of the text is older than the collector?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: state a provisional sense for a term first attested later
questions.stem: A treaty clause turns on a term whose only recorded legal sense appears fifty years after the clause was signed. What is the soundest inference?

options.text: Its sense here is an inference from usage, and should be marked as one
The later sense is certainly the sense the clause intended
options.misconception: assigns a meaning a later text cannot confirm for an earlier one

options.text: The term must be a later copyist's insertion into the clause
options.misconception: invents an interpolation that leaves no sign in the manuscript

options.text: The clause is meaningless, since its key term cannot be fixed
options.misconception: declares a clause void rather than stating a provisional sense

questions.explanation: A term first attested later gives evidence for a range of possible senses at the earlier date, and the sound practice is to fix the sense provisionally from the clause's own usage and to record that reading as provisional. The tempting options adopt the later sense as certain, invent an interpolation that leaves no trace, and throw the clause out instead of stating a cautious reading, which loses an enforceable agreement over a caveat.
questions.hint: What can later usage prove about an earlier clause?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: design a method for comparing totals produced under different rules
questions.stem: Three archives give three totals for one tax year, differing by more than a third. Which step best resolves the disagreement?

options.text: Establish each figure's date, method, and coverage first
Adopt the largest total, since understatement was the usual habit
options.misconception: picks a winner by a general suspicion rather than by method

options.text: Average the three, treating the mean as the truest figure
options.misconception: produces a number that no source ever claimed to record

options.text: Discard whichever total is hardest to explain away
options.misconception: resolves the conflict by preferring whichever figure fits

questions.explanation: Three totals drawn under different rules can be three true statements about different things, and the only way to know whether they conflict is to establish the date, the counting method, and what each set of books actually covered. The tempting options choose by stereotype, average figures whose units are not known to match, and keep whichever total the writer can defend, none of which examines the disagreement at all.
questions.hint: Could all three totals be describing different sets?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain what a source's silence reports about the source
questions.stem: A letter thanks a ruler for safe roads and never mentions the cost of the patrols that kept them clear. What does that silence tell us?

options.text: Only that the writer had no reason to record the levy
That the levies were never collected, since no letter names them
options.misconception: reads one person's silence as the absence of the tax

options.text: That the roads were free, because nobody ever paid for them
options.misconception: infers a zero cost from an unmentioned expense

options.text: That the writer's correspondents had never heard of any tax
options.misconception: extends a private letter's silence across a whole network

questions.explanation: A thank-you note is written about what its writer has cause to be grateful for, and the levy sits outside that purpose, so its silence is evidence about the note rather than about the treasury. The tempting options take the unmentioned levy as uncollected, infer a costless road, and extend one private letter's silence across a whole network of correspondents, none of which the letter's purpose allows.
questions.hint: What was this letter written to do?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: assign each of two documents the question it was made to answer
questions.stem: A monastery chronicle treats a grain seizure as a providential punishment, and the council minute book records the writ, the carts, and the storeroom it filled. Which reading is best?

options.text: The chronicle gives the seizure a moral, the minutes its procedure
The chronicle is reliable because the monks recorded everything
options.misconception: credits a house with total knowledge on the strength of its vows

options.text: The minutes prove the seizure was unlawful, since they record it
options.misconception: reads an administrative record as a legal verdict

options.text: Both show the grain was meant to relieve the shortage
options.misconception: assigns one motive to two texts with different purposes

questions.explanation: The two documents were made for different work, one to place a seizure inside a providential story and one to leave a usable record of carts and storerooms, so each answers a question the other cannot. The tempting options grant the chronicle total recall, read a minute book as a ruling on legality, and attribute a single benevolent motive to texts written for entirely different ends.
questions.hint: What was each office obliged to record?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: state what an unequal survival licenses as a conclusion
questions.stem: After a long war the victors' reports survive in bulk while the defeated side's papers were burned. Which claim about the conflict is most secure?

options.text: The victors' case is better documented than the defeated case
The victors' accounts must be the most accurate of them all
options.misconception: converts a documentary advantage into a claim to truth

options.text: The defeated papers were burned because their side was guilty
options.misconception: makes a missing archive an indictment of the missing side

options.text: The record is balanced, since both sides' words have been found
options.misconception: counts a one-sided survival as though it were even

questions.explanation: When one side's paperwork was deliberately destroyed, the surviving record is a record of the winner's account, and the honest conclusion concerns the visibility of each position rather than the weight of the evidence behind it. The tempting options turn the documentary advantage into a claim of accuracy, read the missing papers as a confession, and call a one-sided archive balanced, which is the conclusion the destruction rules out.
questions.hint: What does the survival rate itself show?
